danish.title: Ellevte bog (1812) — Kapitel 10
paragraphs: Den tredivte august nåede Pierre Moskva. Tæt ved byens porte blev han mødt af grev Rostoptjins adjudant.
»Vi har ledt efter Dem overalt,« sagde adjudanten. »Greven vil særligt gerne tale med Dem. Han beder Dem om straks at komme til ham i en meget vigtig sag.«
Uden at tage hjem tog Pierre en droske og kørte til Moskvas militærguvernør.

Grev Rostoptjin var først den morgen vendt tilbage til byen fra sin sommervilla i Sokolniki. Forværelset og modtagelsesrummet i hans hus var fulde af embedsmænd, der var indkaldt eller var kommet for at hente ordrer. Vasiltjikov og Platov havde allerede talt med greven og forklaret ham, at det var umuligt at forsvare Moskva, og at den måtte overgives. Skønt denne nyhed blev holdt skjult for indbyggerne, vidste embedsmændene — cheferne for de forskellige regeringsafdelinger — at Moskva snart ville være i fjendens hænder, ligesom grev Rostoptjin selv vidste det, og for at undgå personligt ansvar var de alle kommet til guvernøren for at spørge, hvordan de skulle forholde sig med deres respektive afdelinger.
Da Pierre trådte ind i modtagelsesrummet, kom en kurer fra hæren ud af Rostoptjins private gemak.
Som svar på de spørgsmål, han blev mødt med, gjorde kureren en fortvivlet bevægelse med hånden og gik gennem rummet.

Mens han ventede i modtagelsesrummet, betragtede Pierre med trætte øjne de forskellige embedsmænd, gamle og unge, militære og civile, der var til stede. De virkede alle utilfredse og urolige. Pierre gik hen til en gruppe mænd, hvoraf han kendte én. Efter at have hilst på Pierre fortsatte de deres samtale.
»Hvis de bliver sendt af sted og hentet tilbage igen bagefter, skader det ikke, men som tingene er nu, kan man ikke svare for noget.«
»Men ser du, hvad han skriver...« sagde en anden og pegede på et trykt ark, han holdt i hånden.
»Det er en anden sag. Det er nødvendigt for folket,« sagde den første.
»Hvad er det?« spurgte Pierre.
»Åh, det er et nyt opslag.«
Pierre tog det og begyndte at læse.

Hans Højhed er passeret gennem Mosjajsk for at forene sig med tropperne, der rykker frem mod ham, og har indtaget en stærk stilling, hvor fjenden ikke så snart vil angribe ham. Otteogfyrre kanoner med ammunition er sendt derhen herfra, og Hans Højhed siger, at han vil forsvare Moskva til den sidste blodsdråbe og er endog rede til at kæmpe i gaderne. Vær ikke bekymrede, brødre, at domstolene er lukkede; tingene skal nok komme i orden, og vi klarer skurkene på vores egen måde! Når tiden kommer, har jeg brug for både byens og bondens sønner, og jeg vil rejse råbet en dag eller to i forvejen, men de er ikke nødvendige endnu, så jeg tier stille. En økse vil være nyttig, en jagtlanse er ikke dårlig, men en trefork er bedst af alt: en franskmand er ikke tungere end et neg rug. I morgen efter middag tager jeg det Iberiske ikon af Gudsmoderen med til de sårede på Katarina-hospitalet, hvor vi vil lade noget vand velsigne. Det vil hjælpe dem med at komme sig hurtigere. Også jeg er rask nu: det ene øje var ømt, men nu holder jeg udkig med begge.
»Men militærfolk har fortalt mig, at det er umuligt at kæmpe i byen,« sagde Pierre, »og at stillingen...«
»Ja, netop! Det var det, vi sagde,« svarede den første taler.
»Og hvad mener han med 'Det ene øje var ømt, men nu holder jeg udkig med begge'?« spurgte Pierre.

»Greven havde et bygkorn,« svarede adjudanten smilende, »og var meget oprørt, da jeg fortalte ham, at folk var kommet for at spørge, hvad der fejlede ham. Apropos, greve,« tilføjede han pludselig og henvendte sig til Pierre med et smil, »vi har hørt, at De har familieproblemer, og at grevinden, Deres hustru...«
»Jeg har intet hørt,« svarede Pierre ligegyldigt. »Men hvad har De hørt?«
»Åh, De ved jo, hvordan folk er med at digte ting op. Jeg siger bare, hvad jeg har hørt.«
»Men hvad har De da hørt?«
»Tja, man siger,« fortsatte adjudanten med det samme smil, »at grevinden, Deres hustru, forbereder sig på at rejse til udlandet. Jeg formoder, det er vrøvl...«

»Muligvis,« bemærkede Pierre og kiggede fraværende rundt. »Og hvem er dét?« spurgte han og pegede på en lille, ældre mand i en ren blå bondefrakke med et stort, snehvidt skæg og snehvide øjenbryn og et rødmosset ansigt.
»Ham? Det er en købmand, altså, det er restauratøren Veresjtjagin. Måske har De hørt om den historie med proklamationen.«
»Nå, så det er Veresjtjagin!« sagde Pierre og kiggede på det faste, rolige ansigt hos den gamle mand og ledte efter ethvert tegn på, at han var en forræder.
»Det er ikke ham selv, det er faderen til den fyr, der skrev proklamationen,« sagde adjudanten. »Den unge mand sidder i fængsel, og det kommer nok til at gå ham hårdt.«
En ældre herre med en orden og en anden embedsmand, en tysker med et kors om halsen, nærmede sig den talende.

»Det er en indviklet historie, skal jeg sige Dem,« sagde adjudanten. »Proklamationen dukkede op for omkring to måneder siden. Greven blev underrettet. Han gav ordre til at undersøge sagen. Gabriel Ivanovitj her foretog undersøgelserne. Proklamationen var gået gennem nøjagtig treogtres hænder. Han spurgte den ene: 'Hvem har du den fra?' 'Fra den og den.' Han gik til den næste: 'Hvem har du den fra?' og så videre, indtil han nåede til Veresjtjagin, en halvdannet købmand, 'en rigtig petitesse af en handelsmand,' sagde adjudanten smilende. De spurgte ham: 'Hvem har du den fra?' Og pointen er, at vi vidste, hvem han havde den fra. Han kunne kun have fået den fra postmesteren. Men åbenbart var de blevet enige. Han svarede: 'Fra ingen; jeg har selv lavet den.' De truede og forhørte ham, men han holdt fast ved det: 'Jeg har selv lavet den.' Og sådan blev det rapporteret til greven, der sendte bud efter manden. 'Hvem har du proklamationen fra?' 'Jeg har selv skrevet den.' Nå, De kender jo greven,« sagde adjudanten muntert med et stolt smil, »han blev voldsomt hidsig — og tænk bare på fyren, det frækhed, den løgnagtighed og stædighed!«
»Og greven ville have ham til at sige, at den var fra Kljutjarev? Jeg forstår!« sagde Pierre.

»Slet ikke,« svarede adjudanten forskrækket. »Kljutjarev havde sine egne synder at svare for og er derfor blevet forvist. Men pointen er, at greven var meget irriteret. 'Hvordan kan du selv have skrevet det?' sagde han og tog den Hamburgske Avis op, der lå på bordet. 'Her er den! Du har ikke selv skrevet den, men oversat den, og elendigt endda, for du kan ikke engang fransk, din tåbe.' Og hvad tror De? 'Nej,' sagde han, 'jeg har ikke læst nogen aviser, jeg har selv lavet den.' 'Hvis det er tilfældet, er du en forræder, og jeg lader dig stille for retten, og du bliver hængt! Sig, hvem du har den fra.' 'Jeg har ikke set nogen aviser, jeg har selv lavet den.' Og der endte det. Greven lod faderen hente, men fyren holdt fast. Han blev sendt for retten og dømt til strafarbejde, tror jeg. Nu er faderen kommet for at gå i forbøn for ham. Men han er en uduelig knægt! De kender den slags købmandssønner, en laps og en dameven. Han gik til forelæsninger et eller andet sted og bilder sig ind, at fanden selv ikke kan hamle op med ham. Sådan én er han. Hans far har en madsalon her ved Stenbroen, og De ved, der var et stort ikon af Vorherre malet med et scepter i den ene hånd og et rigsæble i den anden. Han tog det ikon med sig hjem i et par dage, og hvad gjorde han? Han fandt en eller anden slyngel af en maler...«

english.title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter 10
paragraphs: On August 30, Pierre reached Moscow. Near the city gates he was met by Count Rostopchin's adjutant.
"We've been looking for you everywhere," said the adjutant. "The count wants to see you urgently. He asks you to come at once on a very important matter."
Without going home, Pierre took a cab and drove to see the Moscow commander in chief.

Count Rostopchin had returned to town from his summer villa at Sokolniki only that morning. The anteroom and reception room of his house were full of officials who had been summoned or had come for instructions. Vasilchikov and Platov had already met with the count and explained that it was impossible to defend Moscow — it would have to be surrendered. Though this news was being kept from the residents, the officials — the heads of the various government departments — knew that Moscow would soon fall to the enemy, just as Rostopchin himself knew it. To avoid personal responsibility, they had all come to the governor to ask how to handle their departments.
As Pierre was entering the reception room, a courier from the army came out of Rostopchin's private room.
In answer to the questions people fired at him, the courier made a despairing gesture with his hand and passed through the room.

While waiting in the reception room, Pierre watched the various officials — old and young, military and civilian — with weary eyes. They all seemed dissatisfied and uneasy. Pierre approached a group of men, one of whom he knew. After greeting Pierre, they continued their conversation.
"If they're sent away and brought back later, no harm done — but as things stand now, nobody can guarantee anything."
"But look at what he writes..." said another, pointing to a printed sheet in his hand.
"That's a different matter. That's meant for the people," said the first.
"What is it?" asked Pierre.
"Oh, another broadsheet."
Pierre took it and began reading.

His Serene Highness has passed through Mozhaysk to join up with the troops moving toward him and has taken up a strong position where the enemy won't attack soon. Forty-eight guns with ammunition have been sent to him from here, and his Serene Highness says he will defend Moscow to the last drop of blood and is even prepared to fight in the streets. Don't worry, brothers — the courts are closed because things need to be put in order, and we'll deal with the criminals our own way! When the time comes I'll call for both townsmen and peasant lads, and I'll raise the cry a day or two beforehand — but they're not needed yet, so I'm holding my tongue. An ax will do nicely, a hunting spear isn't bad, but a three-pronged pitchfork is best of all: a Frenchman is no heavier than a sheaf of rye. Tomorrow after dinner I'll take the Iberian icon of the Mother of God to the wounded at the Catherine Hospital, where we'll bless some water. That will help them get well quicker. I'm well now too — one eye was sore but now I'm keeping watch with both.
"But military men have told me it's impossible to fight in the city," said Pierre, "and that the position..."
"Of course! That's exactly what we were saying," replied the first speaker.
"And what does he mean by 'One eye was sore but now I'm watching with both'?" asked Pierre.

"The count had a sty," the adjutant replied, smiling, "and was very upset when I told him people had been asking what was wrong with him. By the way, Count," he added suddenly, turning to Pierre with a smile, "we hear you have family troubles — that the countess, your wife..."
"I haven't heard anything," Pierre replied indifferently. "But what have you heard?"
"Oh, well, you know how people invent things. I'm only saying what I heard."
"But what did you hear?"
"Well, they say," the adjutant continued with the same smile, "that the countess, your wife, is preparing to go abroad. I'm sure it's nonsense..."
"Possibly," Pierre remarked, looking around absently. "And who is that?" he asked, indicating a short old man in a clean blue peasant coat, with a big snow-white beard and eyebrows and a ruddy face.
"Him? That's a tradesman — the restaurant keeper, Vereshchagin. Maybe you've heard about that business with the proclamation."
"Oh, so that's Vereshchagin!" said Pierre, studying the firm, calm face of the old man and looking for any sign that he might be a traitor.
"That's not the man himself — that's the father of the one who wrote the proclamation," said the adjutant. "The young man is in prison, and I expect things will go badly for him."
An old gentleman wearing a decoration and another official, a German with a cross around his neck, approached the speaker.

"It's a complicated story, you know," said the adjutant. "That proclamation appeared about two months ago. The count was informed and ordered an investigation. Gabriel Ivanovich here made the inquiries. The proclamation had passed through exactly sixty-three hands. He'd ask one person, 'Where did you get it?' — 'From so-and-so.' He'd go to the next — 'Where did you get it?' — and so on until he reached Vereshchagin, a half-educated tradesman, 'a pet of a merchant,' as they say." The adjutant smiled. "They asked him, 'Who gave it to you?' Now the point is, we knew who'd given it to him. He could only have gotten it from the Postmaster. But evidently they'd made some arrangement. He answered: 'From nobody — I wrote it myself.' They threatened and questioned him, but he stuck to his story: 'I wrote it myself.' And so it was reported to the count, who sent for the man. 'Where did you get the proclamation?' — 'I wrote it myself.' Well, you know the count," the adjutant said cheerfully, smiling with pride, "he flew into a terrible rage — just imagine the man's audacity, lying and stubbornness!"
"And the count wanted him to say it came from Klyucharev? I see!" said Pierre.

"Not at all!" the adjutant replied in dismay. "Klyucharev had his own sins to answer for, which is why he was banished. But the point is, the count was furious. 'How could you have written it yourself?' he said, and he grabbed the Hamburg Gazette lying on the table. 'Here it is! You didn't write it — you translated it, and translated it wretchedly, because you don't even know French, you fool!' And what do you think? 'No,' says the man, 'I haven't read any newspapers — I made it up myself.' 'If that's so, you're a traitor and I'll have you tried and hanged! Tell me who gave it to you.' 'I haven't seen any papers — I made it up myself.' And that was the end of it. The count had the father brought in, but the son stuck to his story. He was sent to trial and sentenced to hard labor, I believe. Now the father has come to plead for him. But he's a worthless fellow! You know the type — a tradesman's son, a dandy and ladies' man. He attended some lectures somewhere and thinks the devil himself is no match for him. That's the kind of fellow he is. His father runs a cookshop here by the Stone Bridge, and you know there was a large icon of God Almighty painted with a scepter in one hand and an orb in the other. Well, he took that icon home for a few days, and what did he do? He found some scoundrel of a painter..."
